questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.1 Vision and visual scanning — day vs night vision
questions.keyword: night vision off-center viewing rods cones scotopic photopic
questions.text: A remote pilot conducting an authorized night sUAS operation notices that looking directly at the aircraft's anti-collision light makes it harder to see the aircraft against the dark sky. A colleague suggests looking slightly off-center from the aircraft. What is the physiological basis for this off-center viewing technique?

answers.text: The lens of the eye focuses most accurately on objects located approximately 15 degrees off-center; direct viewing causes focal blur from lens curvature limitations at night

Cone cells concentrated at the fovea provide best color and detail vision in daylight but are insensitive in low light; rod cells distributed around the periphery of the retina are more sensitive to dim light and work better when the image falls off-center
The optic nerve is located at the center of the retina and creates a natural blind spot directly in front of the viewer; off-center viewing avoids this blind spot in all lighting conditions
Off-center viewing activates the parasympathetic nervous system and causes the pupil to dilate more completely, allowing more light to enter the eye for a brighter image

explanations.a: Lens curvature and focal accuracy are not the primary limiting factor in night vision; the distribution of rod versus cone cells is the physiological basis for the off-center viewing technique.
explanations.b: The retina contains two types of photoreceptors: cones, concentrated in the fovea (center), provide sharp color vision in daylight (photopic vision); rods, distributed in the peripheral retina, are far more sensitive to low levels of light and are used in night (scotopic) vision; by looking slightly off-center, the image falls on the rod-rich peripheral retina, making dim objects like aircraft lights more visible in darkness.
explanations.c: The optic disc (blind spot) is located approximately 15 degrees off-center from the fovea, not at the direct center of vision; while the blind spot is a real phenomenon, it is not the reason for off-center viewing in night operations.
explanations.d: While pupil dilation does occur in low light, it is not the mechanism activated by off-center viewing; the benefit of off-center viewing comes from the peripheral rod cell distribution, not from pupil response.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.1 Vision and visual scanning — empty field myopia
questions.keyword: empty field myopia featureless sky blue sky focusing distance
questions.text: A remote pilot is scanning the sky for traffic in a cloudless, featureless blue sky during an sUAS operation at 350 ft AGL. Despite good visual acuity, the pilot fails to notice a distant helicopter at the same altitude. Which visual phenomenon can explain this failure even in good lighting conditions?

answers.text: Fixation error — the pilot's eyes are physically unable to move faster than the angular velocity of the distant helicopter, making detection impossible without optical aids

Empty field myopia — in a featureless visual environment the eyes relax to a resting focal point of approximately 1 to 2 meters rather than focusing at optical infinity, reducing the ability to detect distant objects
Night blindness — the bright blue sky activates the rod suppression reflex, reducing the pilot's ability to detect moving objects in the field of view
Photopic adaptation failure — bright blue sky triggers an overproduction of cone pigments that bleaches out the ability to detect fine contrast differences at range

explanations.a: The human eye can track moving objects across a wide range of angular velocities; failure to detect a distant helicopter is not caused by an eye movement speed limitation.
explanations.b: Empty field myopia occurs when there are no visual cues at varying distances in the field of view; without texture or depth information, the eyes relax to their resting focus distance of approximately 1–2 meters rather than focusing at optical infinity; objects beyond that focal distance, such as a distant aircraft, are slightly blurred and much harder to detect even with good visual acuity under normal conditions.
explanations.c: Night blindness (nyctalopia) is a condition related to low-light or rod cell dysfunction; it is not triggered by a bright blue sky and does not cause the described detection failure in daylight.
explanations.d: Photopic adaptation and cone pigment bleaching occur after exposure to bright light, not as an ongoing response to a uniformly bright sky; this is not the mechanism of empty field myopia.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.1 Vision and visual scanning — effective scan technique
questions.keyword: visual scanning systematic sector technique traffic detection
questions.text: A remote pilot wants to develop an effective visual scanning technique for detecting manned aircraft during sUAS operations. Which scanning approach is most effective for detecting traffic in the visual environment?

answers.text: Fix the gaze at the sUAS at all times; peripheral vision will detect any manned aircraft that enters the field of view without needing to actively scan
Sweep the eyes continuously in a smooth, flowing motion from left to right across the entire field of view at a steady rate
Focus exclusively on the area directly beneath the sUAS flight path because manned aircraft always approach from below when conflicting with sUAS altitude bands
Use a systematic block scanning technique — move the eyes in a series of short, deliberate shifts to successive 10-to-15 degree sectors, pausing briefly in each sector to allow the eye to focus

explanations.a: Fixating on the sUAS while depending on peripheral vision is insufficient for traffic detection; peripheral vision is poor at detecting stationary or slow-moving distant objects and does not substitute for active scanning.
explanations.b: Smooth continuous sweeping is less effective than block scanning because the eyes cannot focus on moving targets during the sweep motion; brief pauses in each sector allow the eye to process detail.
explanations.c: Manned aircraft can approach from any direction and altitude; limiting the scan to the area beneath the sUAS would miss the vast majority of potential conflicts.
explanations.d: The most effective visual scanning technique for detecting traffic uses a systematic block scan with short, deliberate eye movements of 10–15 degrees and a brief pause (about 1 second) in each sector; this allows the eye to focus and process information in each area before moving to the next, maximizing the probability of detecting conflicting traffic.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.2 Spatial disorientation — causes and sUAS implications
questions.keyword: spatial disorientation illusion vestibular misleading visual dominant
questions.text: A remote pilot operating in hazy conditions at dusk loses sight of the horizon. The pilot begins to feel uncertain about the sUAS's attitude based on what the flight controller displays versus what the pilot perceives intuitively. What is the most reliable information source for the remote pilot in this situation?

answers.text: The sUAS flight controller's attitude indicator and telemetry data displayed on the ground control station, which reflects the aircraft's actual orientation
Vestibular (inner ear) sense of balance, which accurately detects aircraft attitude changes even when visual cues are reduced or absent
Kinesthetic sense (feel of the controls), which provides precise attitude feedback through the resistance felt in the control sticks during maneuvering
Peripheral vision, which is more accurate than central vision for detecting attitude deviations in reduced visibility conditions

explanations.a: The sUAS's onboard sensors (IMU, gyroscopes, barometer) feed the flight controller's attitude and telemetry data, which is displayed on the ground control station; this instrumentation is not subject to spatial disorientation and provides the accurate reference when visual cues are lost; the pilot must trust the instruments over subjective sensations.
explanations.b: The vestibular system (inner ear) is unreliable in non-visual conditions; it adapts to sustained motion and can create compelling false sensations of straight-and-level flight when turning, or turning when level — it is the primary cause of spatial disorientation, not a reliable reference.
explanations.c: Kinesthetic sense (control feel) is even less reliable than vestibular sense for detecting aircraft attitude; remote pilots have no physical connection to the aircraft and cannot feel its motion through stick resistance.
explanations.d: Peripheral vision is not more accurate than central vision for attitude detection; in reduced visibility both central and peripheral vision are degraded; instrument data is the reliable reference.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.3 Carbon monoxide — sources symptoms and prevention
questions.keyword: carbon monoxide poisoning symptoms headache confusion impaired judgment
questions.text: A remote pilot is conducting an extended sUAS operation inside a partially enclosed parking structure where a gasoline-powered generator is running nearby. After 45 minutes, the pilot develops a headache, feels mildly confused, and finds it harder to concentrate on the flight. Which hazardous substance is most likely responsible for these symptoms?

answers.text: Carbon monoxide (CO) from the gasoline generator, which displaces oxygen in the blood's hemoglobin and impairs brain function even at low concentrations
Diesel exhaust particulates from vehicles entering the structure, which irritate the bronchial passages and reduce oxygen exchange in the lungs
Ozone produced by the generator's electrical system, which at high concentrations causes respiratory irritation but not the described neurological symptoms
Nitrogen dioxide from exhaust, which causes delayed pulmonary edema but does not produce immediate headache or cognitive impairment in the described timeframe

explanations.a: Carbon monoxide is an odorless, colorless gas produced by incomplete combustion in gasoline engines; CO binds to hemoglobin approximately 200 times more readily than oxygen, preventing oxygen delivery to the brain; early symptoms include headache, confusion, difficulty concentrating, and impaired judgment — all consistent with the described scenario; the pilot must immediately move to fresh air.
explanations.b: Diesel particulates primarily cause respiratory irritation; while they can reduce oxygen exchange, the described rapid onset of headache and cognitive impairment in a partially enclosed space with a running gas generator is more consistent with CO poisoning.
explanations.c: Ozone from electrical equipment is possible but ozone has a distinctive smell; the described combination of headache and cognitive impairment in the context of a gasoline generator is characteristic of CO, not ozone.
explanations.d: Nitrogen dioxide toxicity typically has a delayed presentation (pulmonary edema hours after exposure) and does not cause the immediate headache and confusion described; CO is the more likely cause in this scenario.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.3 Carbon monoxide — sources symptoms and prevention
questions.keyword: CO detector portable alarm enclosed space prevention measure
questions.text: To protect against carbon monoxide exposure during extended sUAS operations in areas where combustion engines are present, which preventive measure is most effective?

answers.text: Wear a surgical face mask rated N95 or higher, which filters CO molecules from the air before they can be inhaled
Conduct operations during the hottest part of the day because heat disperses CO and reduces its concentration at breathing height
Position operations upwind of combustion sources and use a portable battery-powered CO detector/alarm at the operator's position
Limit operations to no more than 15 minutes at a time near any combustion source, then relocate 50 feet away for at least 5 minutes

explanations.a: N95 masks filter particulates but do not filter carbon monoxide, which is a gas; CO passes through particulate filters without reduction.
explanations.b: Temperature does not reliably disperse CO; enclosed or partially enclosed areas can accumulate dangerous CO concentrations regardless of ambient temperature.
explanations.c: Positioning upwind of combustion sources reduces exposure by keeping the operator in cleaner air; a portable CO detector/alarm provides an objective early warning before symptoms develop, since CO is odorless and colorless and cannot be detected by the human senses alone.
explanations.d: A 15-minute rotation schedule provides some reduction in exposure but does not protect against rapid CO accumulation; CO detectors provide far more reliable and timely protection than time-management alone.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.4 Dehydration and heat stress — operational impact
questions.keyword: dehydration heat stress performance degradation pilot vigilance
questions.text: A remote pilot is conducting a 3-hour sUAS agricultural survey in 95°F (35°C) heat with direct sun exposure. The pilot has consumed only a single 12-ounce bottle of water during the entire operation. Near the end of the mission, the pilot makes several inaccurate altitude inputs and fails to notice an aircraft approaching from the south. What physiological condition most likely explains this performance degradation?

answers.text: Dehydration — fluid loss from heat and sweating reduces blood volume and impairs brain function, reducing attention, reaction time, and decision-making quality
Hypoxia — the extreme heat reduces the partial pressure of oxygen at the surface, creating a physiological equivalent of altitude sickness in the field
Hypothermia — despite the ambient heat, evaporative cooling from sweating can cause the core body temperature to drop below normal operating range
Barotrauma — rapid temperature changes between the shaded control station and sun-exposed operating area create pressure differentials that cause inner ear discomfort and loss of concentration

explanations.a: Dehydration reduces blood volume and impairs thermoregulation; even mild dehydration (1–2% of body weight) measurably degrades cognitive performance including attention, reaction time, short-term memory, and decision-making quality — all critical for safe sUAS operations in hot conditions; the pilot must maintain adequate hydration throughout extended outdoor operations.
explanations.b: Hypoxia from surface heat is not a recognized physiological phenomenon; oxygen partial pressure at sea level is not meaningfully affected by ambient temperature in the described range.
explanations.c: Hypothermia requires the core body temperature to fall below 95°F (35°C); sweating in 95°F ambient heat does not cause hypothermia; evaporative cooling regulates temperature toward normal, not below it.
explanations.d: Barotrauma involves pressure differentials in enclosed air spaces such as the middle ear or sinuses; temperature gradients between shaded and sun-exposed areas do not create the pressure changes required for barotrauma.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.5 Stress and performance — inverted U curve Yerkes-Dodson
questions.keyword: stress arousal performance Yerkes-Dodson inverted U optimal range
questions.text: A remote pilot review session covers the Yerkes-Dodson law as it applies to operator performance during sUAS missions. According to this principle, how does the level of stress or arousal affect operational performance?

answers.text: Performance peaks at a moderate level of arousal; too little arousal leads to complacency and inattention, while too much arousal leads to anxiety, tunnel vision, and degraded performance
Performance increases linearly with increasing stress; higher arousal always produces better concentration and faster reaction time regardless of task complexity
Stress has no measurable effect on sUAS operator performance because the external nature of sUAS control insulates the pilot from physiological stress responses
Low arousal always produces the highest performance because calm, relaxed operators make fewer impulsive errors; any arousal above the resting baseline reduces accuracy

explanations.a: The Yerkes-Dodson law describes an inverted U-shaped relationship between arousal and performance: too little arousal produces boredom, complacency, and inattention (low performance); moderate arousal produces optimal alertness and performance; excessive arousal produces anxiety, channelized attention, impaired decision-making, and degraded performance; the goal is to maintain arousal in the optimal moderate range.
explanations.b: The Yerkes-Dodson law specifically contradicts the claim that performance increases linearly with stress; beyond an optimal point, further increases in arousal degrade performance.
explanations.c: sUAS operators are fully subject to physiological stress responses; the external nature of control does not insulate operators from cognitive and physiological effects of stress.
explanations.d: Excessively low arousal reduces vigilance and reaction time; the optimal performance state requires moderate arousal, not resting baseline calm.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.6 Preflight inspection procedures — systematic airframe check
questions.keyword: preflight inspection checklist systematic propeller motor body camera
questions.text: A remote pilot is about to begin a commercial sUAS building inspection. Before each flight, Part 107 requires a safety-focused preflight inspection. Which approach to preflight inspection best satisfies this regulatory requirement and supports safe operations?

answers.text: Use a systematic, written checklist to inspect propellers, motor mounts, airframe, battery connections, camera gimbal, control link, and GPS signal before each flight
Turn on the aircraft and check that all motors spin freely; if no warning lights appear on the GCS, the aircraft is ready to fly
Review the previous flight's logbook to confirm no anomalies were recorded; if the last flight was uneventful, no physical inspection is required for the next flight
Perform the preflight inspection after the first short test hover to confirm the aircraft is responding normally before committing to the full mission

explanations.a: Under 14 CFR 107.49, the remote PIC must ensure the sUAS is in a condition for safe operation before each flight; a systematic written checklist that covers all major components — propellers, motor mounts, airframe integrity, battery connection and charge state, control link function, GPS reception, and payload security — provides the most comprehensive and repeatable preflight assurance.
explanations.b: Checking for warning lights after power-on is one step but is insufficient; structural damage, loose propellers, cracked mounts, and connection issues may not trigger warning lights but can cause in-flight failures.
explanations.c: Previous flight records do not account for damage or changes that may have occurred during transport, storage, or between flights; a physical inspection before each flight is required.
explanations.d: Discovering airworthiness issues during a flight is too late; preflight inspections must be completed before any flight commences, not after a test hover.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.6 Preflight inspection procedures — propeller inspection
questions.keyword: propeller inspection cracks nicks balancing tracking preflight
questions.text: During preflight, a remote pilot inspects the propeller blades on a quadcopter. The pilot finds one blade on a propeller pair has a hairline crack running approximately 5 mm from the root toward the center. The other blade appears undamaged. What action should the pilot take before this flight?

answers.text: Replace the cracked propeller before flying; a hairline crack at the blade root is a structural defect that can propagate under centrifugal loading and cause in-flight propeller failure
Proceed with the flight because a 5 mm crack is within the structural tolerance established by the aircraft manufacturer for normal operations
Replace only the cracked blade while retaining the undamaged blade from the original pair, as mismatched blade replacement restores balance at the lowest cost
Apply cyanoacrylate adhesive to seal the crack and conduct a brief hover test; if no vibration is detected the propeller can remain in service for the current flight

explanations.a: A hairline crack at the propeller root is a serious structural defect; centrifugal forces during high-speed rotation apply enormous stress at the blade root, and a pre-existing crack can rapidly propagate to catastrophic blade separation in flight, causing loss of control and potential injury; the propeller must be replaced before flight.
explanations.b: There is no FAA-recognized structural tolerance for cracks in sUAS propellers; any crack, especially at the blade root where centrifugal and bending stresses are highest, is a disqualifying defect.
explanations.c: Propeller blades must be replaced as matched pairs from the manufacturer; mixing blades from different production batches can introduce imbalance; however, the more fundamental issue is that the cracked blade must be removed regardless.
explanations.d: Field adhesive repair of a cracked propeller blade is not an accepted maintenance practice for sUAS; the repaired blade would not meet the structural integrity required for safe high-speed rotation.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.7 Maintenance records and airworthiness responsibility
questions.keyword: maintenance log sUAS inspection record keeping Part 107 responsibility
questions.text: A remote pilot operates a commercial sUAS for a Part 107 operation. The aircraft was last flown 6 weeks ago and no maintenance log is kept for this aircraft. A propeller replacement was made 3 weeks ago but was not recorded anywhere. Under Part 107 and safe operations principles, what should the operator do differently?

answers.text: Maintain a maintenance log documenting all inspections, repairs, component replacements, and anomalies; this supports airworthiness decisions and provides a history of the aircraft's condition over time
Nothing additional is required because Part 107 does not mandate maintenance logs for sUAS; the pilot needs only to comply with the pre-flight condition check before each flight
File all maintenance records with the FAA within 30 days of each event using the sUAS maintenance portal on the FAA DroneZone website
Submit the aircraft for a biennial condition inspection by a certificated airframe and powerplant (A&P) mechanic to verify it is in safe condition after the 6-week storage period

explanations.a: Maintaining a detailed maintenance log documenting all inspections, repairs, replacements, firmware updates, and anomalies is a best practice that directly supports the Part 107 condition-for-safe-operation requirement; it creates an audit trail, facilitates troubleshooting, and enables informed go/no-go decisions based on aircraft history.
explanations.b: While Part 107 does not mandate the same detailed logbook system as Part 91 for manned aircraft, the regulatory obligation under 107.15 to maintain the aircraft in a condition for safe operation is substantially supported by maintenance records; without logs, the operator cannot reliably track component life, identify recurring problems, or make informed airworthiness decisions.
explanations.c: Part 107 does not require submission of maintenance records to the FAA through DroneZone; maintenance logs are the operator's own documentation tool, not a mandatory FAA reporting instrument.
explanations.d: Part 107 does not require biennial A&P inspections for sUAS; Part 65 A&P mechanics work on type-certificated aircraft; sUAS airworthiness under Part 107 is the remote PIC's responsibility, assessed through preflight inspection and maintained through good maintenance practices.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.8 Post-flight inspection and airworthiness documentation
questions.keyword: post-flight inspection anomaly recording deferred maintenance decision
questions.text: After landing from a mapping mission, a remote pilot notices the sUAS's camera gimbal makes an unusual grinding sound when powered on. The aircraft otherwise functioned normally during the flight. There are no more flights scheduled today. What is the most appropriate action?

answers.text: Log the anomaly in the aircraft maintenance record and have the gimbal inspected and repaired before the next flight to confirm it is in a condition for safe operation
Ignore the anomaly because the camera gimbal is a payload accessory and is not part of the aircraft's airworthiness determination under Part 107
Power cycle the aircraft three times; if the grinding sound does not recur, document it as a transient anomaly and clear the aircraft for the next mission without further action
Continue using the aircraft for the next mission with the grinding gimbal because the problem only affects payload quality, not flight safety

explanations.a: Logging the anomaly immediately after discovery preserves accurate information while the details are fresh; the gimbal should be inspected and repaired before the next flight because a mechanical failure in the gimbal system during flight could affect the aircraft's aerodynamic stability, CG, or payload security under 107.15.
explanations.b: While the gimbal is a payload component, a grinding mechanical failure can propagate, affect CG, detach and strike propellers, or interfere with flight control surfaces; it is not automatically excluded from airworthiness consideration.
explanations.c: A power cycle test is a reasonable first diagnostic step, but the proper response to an anomaly that cannot be explained is to document it and seek inspection before the next flight — not to clear the aircraft based on absence of recurrence in a brief test.
explanations.d: Deferred maintenance on any mechanical anomaly without inspection is inconsistent with the Part 107 obligation to ensure the aircraft is in a condition for safe operation before each flight.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.9 Firmware and software updates — importance and risks
questions.keyword: firmware update flight controller new feature regression testing risk
questions.text: A drone manufacturer releases a firmware update for a popular commercial sUAS that includes improved obstacle avoidance and a new RTH behavior. A remote pilot installs the update overnight before a critical client mission the next morning with no time to test the new firmware. What risk does this approach create?

answers.text: No additional risk; firmware updates from reputable manufacturers are regression-tested before release and the aircraft's behavior is guaranteed to be identical to the previous version
Minimal risk only for night operations; firmware changes do not affect daytime flight characteristics or emergency behaviors

Significant risk that undiscovered behavioral changes in the new firmware could manifest unexpectedly during the client mission, without the pilot having had the opportunity to verify behavior in a low-stakes environment first
The risk is limited to the new RTH behavior; all other flight functions including obstacle avoidance and manual control are unchanged by firmware updates

explanations.a: Even well-tested firmware updates can contain regressions or behavioral changes that interact unexpectedly with specific hardware configurations, environmental conditions, or flight modes; no update is guaranteed to be behaviorally identical to its predecessor.
explanations.b: Firmware changes affect all flight conditions, not only night operations; new RTH behaviors and sensor integration changes can affect any phase of flight.
explanations.c: Installing untested firmware immediately before a critical mission is a significant risk management failure; new firmware can alter RTH behavior, obstacle avoidance response, flight mode characteristics, or other behaviors in ways that have not been verified; best practice requires testing new firmware in a controlled low-stakes environment before using it on client missions.
explanations.d: Firmware updates typically affect the entire flight controller behavior stack, not only the specifically mentioned new features; changes to one area often have cascading effects on other systems.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.6 Preflight inspection procedures — battery inspection and connection
questions.keyword: battery connector XT60 corrosion loose connection resistance heat failure
questions.text: A remote pilot inspects the XT60 battery connector before a flight and notices slight discoloration and pitting on the male pins of the connector. This discoloration indicates the connector has been arcing or experiencing high resistance connections. Under preflight inspection principles, what should the pilot do?

answers.text: Proceed with the flight because minor connector discoloration is cosmetic only and has no effect on current-carrying capacity during normal operations
Apply dielectric grease to the corroded pins to reduce electrical resistance and restore full current capacity before the flight
Replace the damaged connector before flying; a high-resistance or arcing connector can fail under peak current demand, causing power interruption or fire during flight
Test the connection by drawing maximum throttle on the ground for 30 seconds; if no overheating is detected, the connector is safe for flight

explanations.a: Connector discoloration from arcing is not cosmetic; it indicates elevated resistance that generates heat under current load and can progress to connector failure or fire during peak motor demand in flight.
explanations.b: Dielectric grease reduces oxidation but does not restore a connector that has been damaged by arcing; the physical pitting and increased resistance require connector replacement, not lubrication.
explanations.c: A connector showing arcing damage has degraded conductivity; under peak current demand during aggressive maneuvers or hover, the connector can fail catastrophically, causing a sudden power loss that results in loss of control, or can arc severely enough to ignite surrounding materials; the connector must be replaced before flight.
explanations.d: A 30-second ground throttle test does not replicate the peak instantaneous currents drawn during dynamic flight maneuvers; heat buildup may not manifest during the brief test but can cause failure at much higher peak loads in flight.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.10 Propeller and motor maintenance
questions.keyword: motor bearing failure symptoms vibration heat noise early detection
questions.text: A remote pilot performs a manual spin test on each motor during preflight by spinning each propeller by hand with the aircraft powered off. One motor spins smoothly while another produces a rough, grinding feel with slight resistance at one point in the rotation. What does this finding indicate and what should the pilot do?

answers.text: The rough motor is functioning normally; slight resistance in one position is caused by the motor's magnetic detent positions and is expected behavior for all brushless motors
The rough motor has a contaminated rotor; spray electrical contact cleaner into the motor gap and re-test; if the roughness clears, the motor is safe to fly
The resistance indicates the motor stator is magnetized too strongly; the pilot should degauss the motor by spinning it rapidly by hand multiple times before the flight
The rough motor likely has a damaged or worn bearing; continued operation risks bearing seizure in flight, causing that motor to stop producing thrust and destabilizing the aircraft

explanations.a: While brushless motors do have magnetic cogging (detent positions), a distinct rough grinding feel with resistance at a specific point is not normal cogging behavior; it indicates a mechanical problem, most likely a damaged bearing.
explanations.b: Contact cleaner may temporarily mask a bearing problem by displacing contamination without addressing underlying mechanical wear; a motor with grinding sensation requires proper inspection and repair, not a spray-and-test approach.
explanations.c: Degaussing by hand spinning is not a recognized maintenance procedure for brushless motors; magnetic cogging is normal and desired, not a problem requiring correction.
explanations.d: Rough, grinding resistance during manual spin of a brushless motor indicates bearing damage or contamination; a motor with a failing bearing can seize in flight, causing sudden loss of thrust on that motor, which in a quadcopter typically causes loss of control; the motor should be inspected and the bearing replaced or the motor replaced before flight.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.7 Maintenance records and airworthiness responsibility
questions.keyword: airworthiness responsibility remote PIC Part 107 condition safe operation
questions.text: Under 14 CFR Part 107, who bears the final responsibility for determining that an sUAS is in a condition for safe operation before each flight?

answers.text: The aircraft manufacturer, who must certify airworthiness through an annual inspection process equivalent to the Part 91 annual inspection for manned aircraft
The operator's designated maintenance technician, who must sign off on the aircraft's airworthiness before any commercial sUAS flight can legally depart
The remote pilot in command, who is responsible for ensuring the aircraft is in a condition for safe operation before the flight departs
The FAA's Aircraft Registration Branch, which maintains airworthiness records for all registered sUAS and issues flight clearances when records are current

explanations.a: Part 107 does not require an annual inspection process by the manufacturer; airworthiness determination is the remote PIC's responsibility before each flight.
explanations.b: Part 107 does not require a designated maintenance technician to sign off on airworthiness; while qualified maintenance personnel should perform repairs, the pre-flight airworthiness determination is the remote PIC's responsibility.
explanations.c: Under 14 CFR 107.15, the remote pilot in command is responsible for ensuring the sUAS is in a condition for safe operation before each flight; this includes conducting or obtaining a thorough preflight inspection and not flying when a defect could affect safe operation.
explanations.d: The FAA Aircraft Registration Branch maintains registration records, not flight-by-flight airworthiness determinations; there is no FAA flight clearance process for individual Part 107 sUAS operations.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.11 Electromagnetic interference — identification and mitigation
questions.keyword: electromagnetic interference control link frequency 2.4 GHz 5.8 GHz interference sources
questions.text: A remote pilot operating near a large industrial facility begins experiencing intermittent loss of video feed and occasional control link glitches. The pilot suspects electromagnetic interference (EMI). Which field mitigation technique is most likely to reduce the impact of EMI on the control link?

answers.text: Reduce flight altitude to below 50 ft AGL where ground-level shielding from buildings blocks most electromagnetic interference sources
Extend the mission duration to allow the flight controller to adapt to the interference through its automatic frequency hopping calibration routine
Switch the sUAS to attitude mode, which uses less radio bandwidth and is more resistant to electromagnetic interference than GPS-assisted mode
Increase the distance between the transmitter and the interference source, reposition the transmitter antennas toward the aircraft, and if available, switch to a less congested frequency band

explanations.a: Reducing altitude increases proximity to many ground-level interference sources; building shielding is unreliable and reduces VLOS; lower altitude does not systematically reduce EMI.
explanations.b: Flight controller calibration routines do not adapt to EMI interference in real time through an automatic routine; some systems use frequency hopping to find clearer channels, but extending mission duration in an EMI environment worsens the risk rather than resolving it.
explanations.c: Attitude mode reduces GPS dependence but does not reduce radio frequency interference on the control link; the RF link quality is determined by the transmitter/receiver system, not the flight mode selected.
explanations.d: Increasing distance from the interference source reduces signal strength of the interfering signal; repositioning transmitter antennas to point toward the aircraft improves the signal-to-interference ratio; switching between 2.4 GHz and 5.8 GHz (if the system supports it) may find a less congested band; these are the standard field mitigation techniques for EMI-related link issues.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.1 Vision and visual scanning — VLOS maintenance practical limits
questions.keyword: VLOS practical distance size altitude detection capability limitation
questions.text: A remote pilot operating a small 250-gram sUAS estimates it can be seen at distances up to 1,500 feet (approximately 457 meters) in clear daytime conditions. At what distance does the remote pilot begin losing the ability to detect the aircraft's orientation (i.e., which direction it is facing) even if the aircraft is still visible as a dot?

answers.text: At any distance greater than 50 feet, reliable orientation detection is lost; the human eye cannot distinguish front from rear on a small sUAS beyond arm's length
Orientation is unaffected by distance as long as the pilot can see the aircraft; if the aircraft is visible it can always be oriented correctly by the remote pilot

Orientation detection typically degrades well before maximum visibility range; at distances beyond approximately 400 to 600 feet, many small sUAS become difficult to orient reliably without high-visibility coloring, distinctive markings, or movement-based cues
Orientation is always maintained as long as the anti-collision lighting is active because the light flashing pattern indicates nose position to the observer on the ground

explanations.a: 50 feet as the limit for orientation detection is far too conservative; pilots can typically orient their sUAS at much greater distances, though this ability does degrade before maximum visibility is lost.
explanations.b: Orientation is not automatically maintained at all distances where the aircraft is visible; visibility (detecting that the object exists) and orientation (determining which direction it is facing) are separate capabilities that degrade at different rates.
explanations.c: VLOS includes the ability to determine the aircraft's attitude and orientation, not merely its location; for many small sUAS, orientation detection becomes unreliable at distances of 400–600 feet or more, depending on aircraft size, color contrast, and lighting; this is a practical VLOS limitation that pilots should factor into mission planning and maximum operating range decisions.
explanations.d: Anti-collision lights indicate the presence of the aircraft but do not encode nose direction information that can be decoded by a ground observer; flashing patterns are not a standard orientation reference.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.12 Hypoxia — effects at altitude for ground operators
questions.keyword: hypoxia altitude ground operator 8000 feet performance risk
questions.text: A remote pilot team is conducting sUAS surveys at a ground elevation of 9,500 ft MSL in the Rocky Mountains. The remote pilots are operating at this elevation for several hours, controlling sUAS at 9,700 to 9,900 ft MSL. Although hypoxia is typically associated with flight at altitude, how does the elevated ground elevation affect the remote pilot operators themselves?

answers.text: Remote pilots on the ground are unaffected by altitude because they are not flying; hypoxia affects only individuals at altitudes above 12,500 ft MSL inside an unpressurized aircraft

Hypoxia affects remote pilots only if they physically climb above the sUAS's operating altitude; operating at the same or lower elevation as the aircraft prevents any hypoxic effect on the ground crew
The elevated ground elevation actually improves remote pilot performance because the thin air reduces sensory overstimulation and allows for sharper concentration on the GCS display
Ground operators at 9,500 ft MSL can experience mild hypoxic symptoms including reduced reaction time, impaired judgment, and decreased vigilance, which can degrade their sUAS control performance

explanations.a: Hypoxia is not limited to unpressurized aircraft occupants; any person at high altitude — including ground operators — can experience hypoxic effects; 9,500 ft MSL is well within the range where mild hypoxia symptoms can affect performance.
explanations.b: Hypoxia is caused by reduced atmospheric oxygen partial pressure at altitude, not by the person's altitude relative to the aircraft; ground operators at 9,500 ft MSL breathe reduced-oxygen air regardless of where the sUAS is flying.
explanations.c: Thin air does not sharpen concentration; reduced oxygen availability impairs cognitive function rather than improving it; the premise of this option is physiologically incorrect.
explanations.d: At 9,500 ft MSL, the partial pressure of oxygen is approximately 70% of sea-level values; ground operators can experience mild hypoxia symptoms including subtle impairment of judgment, reduced reaction time, decreased vigilance, and increased error rate; these effects are particularly insidious because they develop gradually and the affected person may not recognize their own impairment.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.6 Preflight inspection procedures — control link range check
questions.keyword: range check control link test before flight operational range verification
questions.text: Before beginning an aerial photography mission that will take the sUAS to the limits of VLOS range, a remote pilot conducts a pre-flight range check by walking the transmitter 200 feet from the aircraft with reduced power mode active. The sUAS maintains solid control throughout the range check. What is the purpose of this range check?

answers.text: The range check verifies that the transmitter battery is fully charged and the antenna connections are properly seated before the aircraft is airborne
The range check confirms that the aircraft's GPS satellite acquisition is adequate for the planned automated mission
The range check verifies that the control link performs adequately at a reduced power output, providing confidence that at full power the link will perform reliably at extended operational distances
The range check satisfies the FAA requirement under 14 CFR 107.49 for a documented pre-flight communications system test to be submitted with the flight log

explanations.a: Transmitter battery charge and antenna connections can be checked separately; the specific purpose of a range check with reduced power mode is to verify link quality across distance, not battery or connection status.
explanations.b: GPS acquisition is a separate preflight check; the range check specifically evaluates control link RF performance.
explanations.c: A range check with the transmitter in reduced power mode tests the control link at a fraction of full transmit power; if the link is solid at 200 feet with reduced power, at full power the link should be reliable at much greater distances; this test detects faulty antennas, poor RF connections, or interference before they manifest at operational range.
explanations.d: Part 107 does not require a formally documented pre-flight communications test submission; the range check is a best practice safety procedure, not a regulatory documentation requirement.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.10 Propeller and motor maintenance
questions.keyword: propeller balancing dynamic static balance vibration airframe stress
questions.text: A remote pilot has just replaced a set of propellers on a precision aerial photography sUAS. After replacement, the pilot notices elevated vibration in the gimbal image that was not present before. A technician suggests dynamic propeller balancing. What problem does dynamic propeller balancing address?

answers.text: Dynamic balancing compensates for aerodynamic asymmetry caused by manufacturing tolerances in blade pitch, which affects thrust rather than rotational balance
Dynamic balancing is only relevant for fixed-wing aircraft propellers; multirotor propellers operate at speeds too low for rotational imbalance to produce significant vibration
Dynamic balancing recalibrates the electronic speed controller (ESC) output curves to produce equal thrust from each motor regardless of propeller variation

Dynamic balancing ensures each propeller's mass is evenly distributed around the rotation axis, eliminating the rotating imbalance that causes vibration transmitted through the motor to the airframe and payload

explanations.a: Dynamic balancing addresses mass distribution around the rotation axis, not aerodynamic pitch asymmetry; thrust differences between blades are a separate concern from rotational imbalance.
explanations.b: Multirotor propellers operate at speeds typically between 3,000 and 9,000 RPM, which is more than adequate for rotational imbalance to create significant vibration; dynamic balancing is equally important for multirotor and fixed-wing propellers.
explanations.c: ESC output calibration is a separate electronic procedure from physical propeller balancing; they address different aspects of propulsion performance.
explanations.d: Dynamic propeller balancing uses a balancing tool and vibration sensor to measure and correct uneven mass distribution in the rotating propeller assembly; even small imbalances create centrifugal forces at high RPM that generate vibration, stressing motor bearings, degrading image quality from the camera gimbal, and accelerating airframe fatigue; a properly balanced propeller reduces these effects significantly.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.2 Spatial disorientation — graveyard spiral sUAS analog
questions.keyword: spatial disorientation continued turn illusion sUAS loss visual reference correction
questions.text: A remote pilot operating in reduced visibility loses sight of the sUAS. The GCS telemetry shows the aircraft is in a sustained, banking turn that the pilot did not command. The pilot perceives the aircraft as flying straight and level based on the absence of any control input. What concept does this scenario illustrate and what is the correct action?

answers.text: This illustrates the leans illusion; the pilot should apply opposite rudder input until the GCS attitude indicator shows wings level
This illustrates the graveyard spin; the only recovery is to cut all throttle and allow the aircraft to autorotate to a flat spin before reapplying power
This illustrates mode confusion; the aircraft has entered an unintended GPS orbit mode that will self-correct when GPS signal quality improves

This illustrates how spatial disorientation can cause a pilot to misinterpret aircraft state; the pilot must trust the GCS telemetry and make control inputs to correct the banked turn based on instrument data, not perceived aircraft attitude

explanations.a: The leans is a specific spatial disorientation illusion related to the vestibular system; while related, the broader principle here is that spatial disorientation causes the pilot to misinterpret the aircraft's actual state; the corrective action involves trusting instruments, not specifically rudder input.
explanations.b: Cutting throttle on a multirotor causes uncontrolled descent, not autorotation; autorotation is specific to single-rotor helicopters and is not applicable to multirotors.
explanations.c: The GPS orbit mode would be indicated on the GCS; an uncommanded banked turn without a mode indication is more consistent with a spatial disorientation scenario than a software mode activation.
explanations.d: This scenario illustrates how a remote pilot can lose spatial awareness of an aircraft not in VLOS and experience a form of spatial disorientation — believing the aircraft is in a state different from reality; the correct action is to trust the objective telemetry data from the GCS (attitude indicator, turn rate) and apply the control inputs indicated by the instruments to correct the banked turn, regardless of what the pilot intuitively perceives.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.13 sUAS maintenance — ESC and flight controller care
questions.keyword: ESC electronic speed controller overheating symptom motor stutter failure
questions.text: During a long flight in hot weather, an sUAS begins exhibiting motor stuttering — one motor periodically cuts out briefly before resuming normal operation. A technician later identifies an overheated ESC as the cause. What is the most likely explanation for the ESC overheating?

answers.text: The flight controller software sent incorrect PWM signals to the ESC, causing the ESC to apply reverse voltage that exceeded the thermal rating of the power stage transistors
The battery voltage dropped below the ESC's minimum input voltage threshold, causing the ESC's low-voltage protection circuit to cycle the motor output repeatedly
The ESC's internal clock crystal drifted at high temperature, causing timing errors that created asymmetric PWM signals and intermittent motor communication loss
The ESC exceeded its continuous current or temperature rating due to high ambient temperature combined with high motor demand, causing the ESC's thermal protection to momentarily throttle output

explanations.a: Flight controller PWM signal errors would produce consistent incorrect behavior across all conditions, not temperature-dependent intermittent stuttering; reverse voltage signals are also not a standard flight controller malfunction pattern.
explanations.b: Battery low-voltage protection would affect all motors simultaneously and consistently, not intermittently on one motor; the temperature correlation makes ESC thermal protection the more likely explanation.
explanations.c: Clock crystal drift causing timing errors is not a standard ESC failure mode in this context; ESC timing is handled digitally and does not produce the described thermal symptom pattern.
explanations.d: ESCs have maximum continuous current ratings and thermal limits; in hot ambient conditions with high motor demand (heavy payload, aggressive flight, high altitude), ESCs can exceed their thermal rating, activating the built-in thermal protection circuit that momentarily reduces or cuts output to prevent component damage; this manifests as motor stuttering and is a clear sign the ESC is operating beyond its design envelope.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.9 Firmware and software updates — flight controller calibration
questions.keyword: IMU calibration accelerometer gyroscope level surface procedure
questions.text: A remote pilot's flight controller manual requires an IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit) calibration after a firmware update or following any significant impact or crash. Why is IMU calibration important for safe sUAS operation?

answers.text: IMU calibration updates the aircraft's GPS waypoint database and is required to access newly surveyed airspace grids in the flight controller's mapping system
IMU calibration is only required after crashes; firmware updates do not alter IMU sensor characteristics and do not necessitate recalibration
IMU calibration resets the battery cell balance data stored in the flight controller's memory, preventing false low-battery warnings after firmware changes

IMU calibration aligns the accelerometer and gyroscope sensors to a known level reference, ensuring the flight controller correctly interprets sensor data to maintain stable flight and accurate attitude control

explanations.a: IMU calibration is a sensor alignment procedure, not a GPS database update; airspace grid data is updated through separate map or firmware processes.
explanations.b: Firmware updates can change how sensor data is processed or interpreted, potentially requiring recalibration to ensure sensor readings are correctly applied by the new firmware; manufacturer guidance typically specifies when recalibration is needed.
explanations.c: Battery cell balance data is managed by the battery management system and charger, not the flight controller's IMU calibration routine.
explanations.d: The IMU contains accelerometers (measuring linear acceleration) and gyroscopes (measuring rotational rate); calibration establishes accurate reference values for these sensors relative to a known level surface; after a firmware update or impact, sensor offset values may need to be re-established so the flight controller correctly interprets sensor inputs for attitude control, hover stability, and autonomous flight.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.4 Dehydration and heat stress — prevention strategies
questions.keyword: heat illness heat stroke heat exhaustion symptoms prevention recognition
questions.text: A remote pilot supervising a full-day summer sUAS survey operation in direct sunlight notices a crew member becoming confused, having hot and dry skin, and complaining of severe headache. The crew member's skin is flushed but not sweating despite the 98°F (37°C) ambient temperature. What emergency condition may this describe and what is the immediate response?

answers.text: Heat exhaustion — the crew member should be given a cold sports drink and rest for 15 minutes in the shade before resuming work
Mild dehydration — the crew member should drink two bottles of water and continue working at a reduced pace
Heat stroke — a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate cooling (ice packs to neck, armpits, and groin), removal from heat, and immediate activation of emergency medical services
Hyperventilation — the crew member is breathing too rapidly in the heat; a paper bag technique should be used to restore CO₂ balance before resuming operations

explanations.a: Heat exhaustion is characterized by heavy sweating, weakness, and cool, pale, moist skin; the described combination of confusion, hot dry skin, and cessation of sweating indicates heat stroke, not heat exhaustion — a much more severe and immediately life-threatening condition.
explanations.b: Mild dehydration does not cause confusion and cessation of sweating; these signs indicate heat stroke requiring emergency intervention, not simply rehydration and continued work.
explanations.c: The described symptoms — confusion, hot and dry skin, flushing, absence of sweating despite extreme heat — are classic signs of heat stroke, a life-threatening medical emergency; the body has lost the ability to regulate temperature; immediate aggressive cooling and emergency medical services are required; delay can result in organ failure or death.
explanations.d: Hyperventilation produces tingling, dizziness, and spasms but not hot dry skin and confusion; heat stroke is the correct identification requiring emergency cooling and EMS activation.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.11 Electromagnetic interference — identification and mitigation
questions.keyword: GPS jamming GNSS interference altitude behavior position error visual reference
questions.text: During a GPS-assisted automated sUAS mission near a military installation, the aircraft begins drifting slowly in one direction and the GCS shows GPS accuracy degrading with increasing position error radius. The pilot suspects GPS jamming. What immediate action should the pilot take?

answers.text: Increase the sUAS altitude immediately; GPS jamming is only effective below 200 ft AGL and climbing above this threshold restores normal GPS reception
Switch to manual or attitude mode, take manual control of the aircraft, and navigate it back to the landing zone using visual reference before GPS loss becomes complete
Activate the emergency RTH mode, which uses Galileo satellite signals that are immune to GPS jamming because they operate on a different frequency
Hover the aircraft in place and wait; GPS accuracy degrades cyclically and will recover within 5 minutes when the jamming frequency shifts

explanations.a: GPS jamming is not altitude-limited to 200 ft AGL; military-grade jammers affect all altitudes within their effective radius; climbing does not restore GPS reception.
explanations.b: When GPS accuracy is degrading and jamming is suspected, the pilot should immediately switch to manual/attitude mode to take direct control before GPS loss is complete; navigating visually back to the landing zone while the aircraft is still maneuverable and in VLOS is the safest response to GNSS degradation.
explanations.c: RTH requires GPS navigation; in a GPS-jammed environment, RTH cannot function reliably; Galileo satellite signals are in a different frequency band but can also be jammed; no satellite navigation system is immune to dedicated jamming.
explanations.d: GPS jamming does not cycle predictably in short 5-minute windows; waiting in a hover while GPS degrades risks a GPS-loss event that causes the aircraft to drift uncontrollably before the pilot can intervene.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.5 Stress and performance — acute stress response management
questions.keyword: startle response acute stress physiological recovery controlled breathing
questions.text: A remote pilot experiences a sudden close approach by an unexpected helicopter, triggering an acute startle response that causes the pilot to momentarily freeze on the controls. After the helicopter passes safely, the pilot notices elevated heart rate, shaking hands, and difficulty concentrating. How should the pilot manage this acute stress response before resuming critical flight operations?

answers.text: Immediately resume full flight operations at maximum capability to overcome the startle response through forced engagement; hesitation worsens acute stress
Take a brief pause, use controlled breathing techniques to reduce physiological arousal, allow the acute response to subside, and reassess situational awareness before resuming complex operations
Transfer control to the visual observer immediately; once a startle response has occurred, the remote PIC is legally required to hand off control under the emergency deviation provision
Reduce altitude to 100 ft AGL and maintain a hover until heart rate drops below 100 beats per minute, then resume full operations per standard procedure

explanations.a: Forcing immediate full engagement after a startle response does not allow the physiological stress response to subside; cognitive performance is degraded immediately after acute stress and complex operations should be delayed until recovery occurs.
explanations.b: After an acute startle event, the physiological stress response (elevated heart rate, adrenaline release, trembling) takes several minutes to subside; controlled breathing (slow deep breaths) helps activate the parasympathetic system to reduce heart rate and arousal; taking a pause to reassess the situation and allow recovery before resuming complex maneuvers is sound human factors practice.
explanations.c: Emergency deviation under 107.21 applies to in-flight emergencies, not to the aftermath of a startle event; there is no regulatory requirement to transfer control after a startle response.
explanations.d: Hovering at 100 ft AGL is a reasonable stabilizing action, but the specific heart rate threshold and altitude requirement described are not based on FAA guidance; the key is a managed recovery period before resuming complex operations.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.8 Post-flight inspection and airworthiness documentation
questions.keyword: post-flight log battery cycle count capacity check long-term health tracking
questions.text: After completing a series of commercial sUAS flights, a remote pilot logs the total flight time and notes the battery cycle count in the maintenance record. Why is tracking battery cycle count important for sUAS airworthiness?

answers.text: Battery cycle count determines the FAA registration expiration date; batteries used more than 150 cycles require re-registration under Part 48

LiPo batteries have a limited cycle life; tracking cycle count helps the operator identify when a battery is approaching the end of its usable service life and should be retired before it causes an in-flight power failure
Cycle count is tracked exclusively for warranty purposes; it has no relationship to the battery's actual remaining capacity or reliability in service
FAA regulations require battery cycle count to be reported quarterly to the manufacturer as part of the Part 107 safety monitoring program

explanations.a: Battery cycle count has no connection to FAA registration expiration; Part 48 registration expiration is time-based (3 years), not cycle-based.
explanations.b: LiPo batteries degrade chemically with each charge-discharge cycle; after a certain number of cycles (typically 150–300 for most commercial sUAS batteries, depending on manufacturer and usage intensity), capacity and peak discharge capability decline significantly; tracking cycle count allows the operator to retire batteries proactively before degraded performance causes an in-flight power failure.
explanations.c: Cycle count is operationally relevant for capacity and reliability planning, not only for warranty claims; ignoring cycle count until failure occurs is a reactive rather than proactive maintenance approach.
explanations.d: Part 107 does not establish a quarterly battery cycle count reporting requirement to manufacturers; maintenance records are the operator's own documentation tool.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.13 sUAS maintenance — crash inspection protocol
questions.keyword: post-crash inspection mandatory components before return to service
questions.text: An sUAS experiences a hard landing that cracks one landing gear arm. The aircraft appears otherwise undamaged and still powers on normally. The pilot wants to fly again later that day after replacing only the cracked landing gear. What additional post-crash inspections are required before the aircraft can return to service?

answers.text: No additional inspection is needed beyond replacing the visible cracked part; if all motors spin and the GCS shows no errors, the aircraft is ready to fly after the gear repair

The aircraft should undergo a thorough inspection of all components potentially affected by the impact, including propellers, motor mounts, airframe structure, battery connection, and flight controller calibration, before returning to flight
Only the battery needs to be inspected after a hard landing; impact damage to structural components does not affect electronic systems in well-designed sUAS
The aircraft should be sent to the manufacturer for factory inspection after any hard landing; field post-crash inspection is not adequate for Part 107 commercial operations

explanations.a: Visible damage rarely tells the complete story; impact forces from a hard landing propagate through the structure and can damage motor mounts, create micro-cracks in propellers, loosen battery connections, disturb IMU calibration, or crack the PCB of the flight controller; a single-item repair without comprehensive inspection risks a secondary failure in flight.
explanations.b: Post-crash inspection requires systematic evaluation of all components that could have been affected by the impact forces: propellers for cracks or chips, motor mounts for bending or loosening, airframe for delamination or cracks, battery connection for loosening or arcing damage, battery for puffing, and flight controller sensors for calibration drift; only a comprehensive inspection supports a confident return-to-service decision.
explanations.c: Impact forces transmit through the entire structure and can affect any component; electronic components including flight controllers and ESCs can be damaged by impact shock independent of visible damage to structural parts.
explanations.d: Manufacturer factory inspection for every hard landing is not required by Part 107; the remote PIC is responsible for ensuring the aircraft is in a condition for safe operation, which is accomplished through a thorough field inspection augmented by qualified technician support when needed.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.1 Vision and visual scanning — color vision limitations
questions.keyword: color blindness sUAS navigation light recognition limitation Part 107
questions.text: A remote pilot candidate who has a red-green color vision deficiency wants to know whether this condition affects their eligibility for a Part 107 Remote Pilot Certificate. How does Part 107 address color vision requirements?

answers.text: Part 107 requires normal color vision as a prerequisite for certification; applicants with red-green color blindness are ineligible for a Remote Pilot Certificate and must apply for a waiver

Part 107 does not require any specific color vision standard; unlike manned aircraft medical certificates, there is no FAA medical requirement for remote pilot certification, and color vision is not a stated eligibility criterion
Part 107 requires a minimum of 20/40 corrected visual acuity and normal color vision as measured by the Ishihara plate test administered by an Aviation Medical Examiner
Part 107 requires normal color vision for night operations only; daytime operations are not subject to any color vision standard

explanations.a: Part 107 does not require normal color vision as an eligibility criterion; the absence of FAA medical requirements for remote pilots means that color vision deficiency does not automatically disqualify an applicant.
explanations.b: Part 107 does not require an FAA medical certificate or any specific color vision standard; the eligibility requirements at 107.61 focus on age (16 minimum), English language proficiency, and mental/physical fitness to operate the sUAS safely; a person with color vision deficiency is not categorically barred from certification.
explanations.c: There is no Ishihara plate test requirement or 20/40 acuity standard administered by an AME for Part 107 certification; these are manned aviation medical certificate requirements that do not apply to remote pilots.
explanations.d: Part 107 does not differentiate color vision requirements between day and night operations; no color vision standard is specified for either condition.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.6 Preflight inspection procedures — GPS and compass check
questions.keyword: GPS satellite acquisition HDOP preflight check minimum satellites acceptable
questions.text: A remote pilot prepares to launch an sUAS for an automated waypoint mission. The GCS shows the aircraft has acquired 6 GPS satellites but the GPS accuracy indicator shows a poor HDOP value of 4.2. The manufacturer's manual recommends a minimum of 8 satellites and HDOP below 2.0 for automated missions. Should the pilot proceed?

answers.text: Yes, because 6 satellites meets the absolute minimum for 3D position fix and HDOP below 5.0 is acceptable for civilian GPS receivers
Yes, if the automated mission is limited to altitudes below 200 ft AGL where GPS geometry errors are smallest

No, the manufacturer's minimum specifications of 8 satellites and HDOP below 2.0 are not met; proceeding with an automated GPS mission in these conditions risks position errors that could cause the aircraft to fly an incorrect path
No, but only if the mission crosses into controlled airspace; automated missions in Class G airspace can proceed with any number of satellites above 4

explanations.a: While 6 satellites can provide a 3D fix, the manufacturer's recommended minimums are based on the GPS accuracy needed for reliable automated flight; HDOP of 4.2 indicates poor geometric quality of satellite positions, which translates to larger position errors.
explanations.b: Altitude does not significantly affect GPS geometry errors; HDOP is a function of satellite geometry in the sky, not the aircraft's altitude above ground.
explanations.c: The manufacturer's recommended minimums for automated missions (8 satellites, HDOP < 2.0) represent the conditions under which the flight controller is designed to perform reliably; the current conditions (6 satellites, HDOP 4.2) fall below both criteria; proceeding with the automated mission risks position errors that cause the aircraft to fly off its intended path, potentially into unauthorized areas or toward obstacles.
explanations.d: Airspace class does not determine whether GPS conditions are adequate for an automated mission; the manufacturer's performance specifications apply regardless of airspace class.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.14 Noise and vibration — effects on remote pilot over extended operations
questions.keyword: vibration noise prolonged exposure hearing protection fatigue performance
questions.text: A remote pilot operates a fleet of sUAS commercially for 8 to 10 hours per day, six days per week. The aircraft produce significant rotor noise at approximately 85 dB at the operator's position. Over several months, the pilot notices a persistent ringing in the ears (tinnitus) and difficulty understanding speech in noisy environments. What occupational health issue is developing, and what protective measure should be implemented?

answers.text: The pilot is experiencing middle ear barotrauma from repeated pressure changes as sUAS climb and descend near the operator; pressurization through yawning resolves the condition without additional protection

The pilot is developing noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL) from prolonged exposure to high-decibel rotor noise; hearing protection rated for the specific decibel exposure level should be worn during all extended sUAS operations

The tinnitus is caused by electromagnetic interference from the transmitter operating at close range; switching to a lower-power transmission mode reduces the electromagnetic exposure and resolves the condition
The pilot is developing a stress response to the monotonous sound of the rotors; environmental sound masking with music at equal volume through earbuds will resolve the condition

explanations.a: Barotrauma results from pressure differential in enclosed air spaces such as the sinuses and middle ear; it produces pain and muffled hearing, not tinnitus and progressive hearing loss from occupational noise exposure.
explanations.b: Noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL) results from prolonged exposure to sound levels at or above 85 dB; the described symptoms of tinnitus and speech discrimination difficulty are classic early signs of NIHL; OSHA standards recommend hearing protection for continuous exposure at 90 dB for 8 hours, and the risk increases at higher levels; appropriate hearing protection (earplugs or earmuffs rated for the measured exposure level) should be worn during extended sUAS operations.
explanations.c: Electromagnetic fields from transmitters operating at typical sUAS control frequencies do not cause tinnitus or hearing loss; the source is acoustic noise, not electromagnetic exposure.
explanations.d: Sound masking at equal volume would add to the total sound exposure rather than reducing it; adding music at 85 dB to existing 85 dB rotor noise creates 88 dB combined exposure, worsening the problem.

questions.name: Physiology and Maintenance
questions.objective: 9.6 Preflight inspection procedures — systematic final check before flight
questions.keyword: before takeoff final check mission brief crew coordination launch authorization
questions.text: Immediately before launching an sUAS for a commercial inspection flight, a remote pilot completes a final before-takeoff check. Beyond confirming aircraft airworthiness and weather conditions, which additional elements should this final check include?

answers.text: Contact the FAA Command Center to receive a verbal operations authorization confirmation for the planned flight before the aircraft is launched

Confirm airspace authorization is valid and current, verify the flight crew understands their roles, confirm the landing zone and emergency landing zone are clear, and confirm battery charge is adequate for the planned mission plus reserve
Confirm the aircraft's transponder is set to Mode C and squawking 1200, and that ATIS information for the nearest airport has been received and acknowledged
File a real-time flight notification with the FAA's UAS Facility Map system to alert nearby aircraft of the imminent sUAS launch

explanations.a: There is no FAA Command Center verbal authorization process for standard Part 107 commercial flights; airspace authorization is obtained through LAANC or DroneZone prior to the operation, not at launch.
explanations.b: A comprehensive before-takeoff check includes: confirming that any required airspace authorization is valid for the current time window, briefing all crew members on their roles and the flight plan, confirming the landing zone and designated emergency landing zone are clear of people and obstacles, and verifying that battery charge is sufficient for the mission with the required reserve — all critical elements that directly support safe flight operations.
explanations.c: Part 107 prohibits transponders and ADS-B Out on sUAS; there is no transponder check for sUAS; ATIS check is a manned aviation pre-departure procedure that does not apply to the sUAS launch process.
explanations.d: There is no FAA real-time launch notification system that remote pilots are required to file immediately before launch; LAANC authorization is obtained in advance and no additional launch notification to a UAS Facility Map is required.
